findings.summary: Cellular automaton is a discrete computation model of a regular grid of cells that evolve through time via a fixed rule applied simultaneously to all cells. Each cell's new state depends on its current state and the states of cells in its defined neighborhood. Originating in the 1940s at Los Alamos with Ulam and von Neumann, the framework expanded through studies of crystal growth, self-replication, and excitable media. Stephen Wolfram later classified one-dimensional rules into four classes, with Class 4 supporting complex, persistent structures thought to be computationally universal. Well-known examples include Conway's Game of Life and Rule 110, which can simulate Turing machines. Simulations typically use finite grids with periodic boundary conditions to avoid edge effects, enabling programmable modular arithmetic implementations.

mechanisms.title: Cell state update via fixed rule
mechanisms.explanation: Each cell updates its state simultaneously according to a deterministic mathematical function that considers the cell's current state and the states of cells in its neighborhood. The rule is applied uniformly across the grid, though exceptions such as stochastic or asynchronous variants exist.

mechanisms.title: Neighborhood-defined interaction
mechanisms.explanation: A cell's next state is determined by a configured neighborhood of adjacent cells. Common neighborhood types include von Neumann (orthogonal only) and Moore (orthogonal plus diagonals). The size and shape of the neighborhood directly affect the total number of possible automata configurations.
